paper_title: Game2Real-Bench: Do Toy Games Reveal and Transfer to Real-World Visual Reasoning?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on either real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve the complexity of natural scenes, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether the abilities measured in toy games correspond to those required in real-world visual reasoning, and whether game examples can provide useful signals for solving real-world tasks. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, benchmark for studying these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. On the game side, we construct 1,000 independently generated samples from executable task specifications and verify their answers programmatically. On the real-world side, we curate and construct 400 samples from diverse real-world sources. We connect the two settings according to shared reasoning requirements, including visual evidence, spatial operations, constraints, and state transitions, rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs across both settings. Performance on game and real-world tasks shows consistent cross-setting trends, with Pearson correlation of 0.935 and Spearman correlation of 0.935. We further examine game-to-real transfer through one-shot in-context learning on four models. The effect varies across capabilities and models. Constraint reasoning shows positive gains for several models, while fine-grained perception consistently declines with game demonstrations. These results show that toy games can reflect some reasoning patterns observed in real-world tasks and can provide useful demonstrations in selected settings. To further support model training, we construct Game2Real-Dataset, comprising nearly 24K game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. These samples are generated from executable task specifications and verified programmatically. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have led to substantial progress in multimodal understanding and reasoning (Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2026a;c). Beyond recognizing what is present in an image, visual reasoning requires models to understand how objects are related, how constraints interact, and how actions change scene. These demands arise in everyday tasks, such as interpreting an assembly step, as well as in toy games with explicit rules and controllable states. Games are particularly appealing because their tasks can be generated at scale and their answers verified programmatically (Tong et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Yet their simplified visual environments raise central question: Do toy games reveal VLMs real-world visual reasoning capabilities, and can solved game examples support transfer to real-world tasks? Existing benchmarks characterize different aspects of visual reasoning. MMMU and MMERealWorld cover knowledge-intensive problems and real-world scenarios (Yue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), while BLINK and BabyVision reveal weaknesses in foundational visual skills despite Equal contribution. Correspondence to haiwen.diao@ntu.edu.sg Preprint. strong high-level reasoning performance (Fu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026). Recent work shows that procedural tasks can support reasoning beyond their original settings: Game-RL improves VLM reasoning through game-based training (Tong et al., 2026), and VBVR-Pro demonstrates transfer to external reasoning benchmarks for visual generation models (Xu et al., 2026). These findings highlight the potential of procedural training, but leave open how game-based assessment relates to real-world reasoning across models and capabilities. shared evaluation linking tasks by their reasoning requirements is needed to examine this relationship and the usefulness of game examples. To this end, we introduce Game2Real-Bench, benchmark linking toy games and real-world visual reasoning across four capabilities: Fine-grained Perception, Spatial Reasoning, Constraint Reasoning, and Sequential Planning. We construct the game evaluation using executable generators and task-specific verifiers, and curate real-world tasks according to shared reasoning requirements rather than visual resemblance (Figure 1). The resulting benchmark combines 1,000 independently generated and programmatically verified toy-game samples with 400 real-world samples derived from images, videos, and multi-view observations. The same pipeline produces Game2Real-Dataset, separate collection of nearly 24K verified samples spanning 18 toy-game tasks and 65 questionanswer (QA) families, providing scalable resource for visual reasoning evaluation and training. Our evaluation of 25 representative VLMs reveals strong correspondence between game and realworld performance, with model-level Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. Despite their simpler visual environments, game tasks are generally harder and better distinguish models. The benefits of game examples are more selective. In one-shot in-context learning with four models, randomly selected game demonstrations improve constraint reasoning for several models but lower fine-grained perception accuracy for all four, with slight decline in average overall accuracy. These findings suggest that toy games are informative probes of real-world visual reasoning, while their usefulness as demonstrations depends on the capability and model. We further analyze thinking mode and recurring failures in spatial representation, relational consistency, and state updating. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Game2Real-Bench, 1,400-sample benchmark that aligns toy-game and real-world tasks through shared reasoning requirements across four capabilities, enabling analysis of cross-setting performance correspondence and game-to-real transfer. We construct Game2Real-Dataset, comprising nearly 24K programmatically verified samples across 18 toy-game tasks and 65 QA families, together with executable generators and task-specific verifiers to support future research on scalable visual reasoning. We evaluate 25 VLMs, revealing strong gamereal performance correspondence and selective one-shot transfer, with analyses of thinking mode and reasoning failures.

sections.title: 2.1 GAMES AS TESTBEDS FOR VISUAL REASONING
sections.content: Recent work has increasingly used games and procedural environments as testbeds for multimodal reasoning, benefiting from their explicit rules, controllable states, and verifiable outcomes. In interactive settings, benchmarks such as BALROG, LMGame-Bench, VideoGameBench, and GameWorld use diverse games to evaluate perception, planning, memory, and decision making in LLM and VLM agents (Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a; Ouyang et al., 2026). Beyond evaluation, games have also been used to construct reasoning tasks and training supervision. Game-RL synthesizes verifiable multimodal reasoning problems from game mechanics, while Play to Generalize investigates whether reasoning abilities acquired through gameplay transfer to broader multimodal tasks (Tong et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026b). VBVR-Pro further scales procedural visual reasoning to broad collection of automatically generated tasks with task-specific verification (Xu et al., 2026). Together, these studies establish games and procedural environments as effective testbeds for multimodal reasoning. However, their relationship to real-world reasoning is typically assessed indirectly, either through in-game performance or aggregate results on external benchmarks. Game2Real-Bench makes this relationship explicit by organizing procedurally generated game tasks and real-world samples around shared reasoning requirements, enabling analysis of cross-setting performance correspondence and game-to-real transfer at the capability level. 2 Figure 1: Multi-stage construction pipeline of Game2Real-Bench. It comprises capability-guided task design, procedural generation and verification, and mechanism-aligned real-world curation.

sections.title: 2.2 BENCHMARKS FOR VISUAL REASONING
sections.content: Recent advances in encoder-based and encoder-free VLMs (Diao et al., 2024; 2025) have improved visual perception, understanding, and multimodal reasoning. To evaluate these capabilities, wide range of benchmarks have been proposed. General-purpose benchmarks such as MMMU and MMERealWorld assess multimodal reasoning across knowledge-intensive and complex real-world scenarios (Yue et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), while vision-centric benchmarks such as BLINK, MMVP, and BabyVision focus more directly on visual perception and reasoning with reduced reliance on external knowledge (Fu et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026). Other benchmarks study more structured forms of visual reasoning, including 3D understanding, multi-view reasoning, spatial relations, and logical constraints (Jia et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Xie et al., 2026a). Recent work has also explored synthetic and procedural tasks for controlled visual reasoning. CLEVR uses synthetic scenes to study compositional visual reasoning (Johnson et al., 2017), while later efforts such as Game-RL, VBVR, and VBVR-Pro extend procedural generation to broader reasoning tasks, games, and training settings (Tong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). These settings enable precise control over task structure and reliable solution generation at scale. However, it is still not well understood whether the capabilities reflected by procedurally generated games correspond to those required by real-world visual reasoning. Game2Real-Bench studies this relationship by combining game and real-world visual reasoning tasks under shared capability framework, allowing us to examine both cross-setting performance consistency and game-to-real transfer.

sections.title: 3 GAME2REAL-BENCH
sections.content: We construct Game2Real-Bench in three stages, as illustrated in Figure 1. In Stage 1, we organize the task space around four capability groups and design 18 toy-game tasks with 65 QA families. In Stage 2, we develop executable generators and task-specific verifiers to construct Game2RealDataset with 23,893 verified game samples, while independently generating 1,000 samples for the toy-game evaluation set. In Stage 3, we curate 400 real-world samples that require reasoning operations corresponding to those exercised by the toy games. The outputs of Stages 2 and 3 together constitute the complete 1,400-sample Game2Real-Bench. We describe each stage in detail below.

sections.title: 3.1 TASK DESIGN
sections.content: Taxonomy. We organize Game2Real-Bench around four complementary capabilities in visual reasoning and design 18 toy-game tasks accordingly. Fine-grained Perception requires models to identify task-relevant visual evidence from subtle local differences, correspondences, and partial observations. Spatial Reasoning requires models to infer and transform spatial configurations involving relations, orientation, viewpoint, geometry, and 3D structure. Constraint Reasoning requires models to integrate multiple interdependent relations and constraints to derive globally consistent solution. Sequential Planning requires models to reason over state transitions and select 3 Figure 2: Capability-aligned tasks in Game2Real-Bench. Toy-game and real-world tasks span fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We present representative QA samples illustrating shared reasoning requirements across the two settings. state-dependent actions toward target goal. Individual tasks may involve multiple capabilities, and each task is assigned to the group that best reflects its primary reasoning demand. Task and QA Formulation. In Game2Real-Bench, toy-game task defines structured visual reasoning problem with explicit rules and solution criteria, while its QA families specify the reasoning targets and output formats. These QA families cover fine-grained visual evidence, spatial relations and transformations, constraint-consistent configurations, and action selection over evolving states. Across the 18 tasks, we define 65 QA families in open-ended and multiple-choice formats. sample is generated from task configuration and contains one or more visual observations, question, and verified answer. The corresponding QA family further specifies any task-specific notation, coordinate system, and output convention, ensuring consistent evaluation across generated samples.

sections.title: 3.2 PROCEDURAL GENERATION
sections.content: Design Principles. Our procedural generation follows three principles. Visual Grounding. Each question is designed so that its answer is determined by the visual content rather than prompt wording. The text specifies the task and rules, while the image provides the instance-specific evidence required to solve it. Diversity. We vary problem structures, spatial layouts, and visual presentations across generated instances while preserving the underlying task rules and reasoning objective, producing diverse instances of the same capability. Verifiability. Each problem follows explicit executable rules, allowing the correct solution to be derived and checked programmatically. Instance Generation. For each task, we implement task-specific generator that samples valid problem states from predefined configuration ranges. Given sampled state and QA family, the generator jointly produces the visual observations, question, and ground-truth answer. Structural parameters control factors such as topology, object configurations, constraints, paths, and state transitions, while presentation parameters determine how each state is visually encoded and rendered. We also retain the structured metadata required for verification, analysis, and de-duplication. Programmatic Verification. Each task is paired with deterministic solver or verifier tailored to its solution structure. Verification may involve constraint solving, geometric transformation, state simulation, graph search, or transition replay. Given the sampled state, the verifier recomputes the requested result or checks the proposed solution against executable task rules. For tasks requiring uniqueness, alternative valid solutions are explicitly checked; when multiple solutions are permitted, all admissible answers are retained. When optimality is required, the answer is checked against the 4 solver-derived optimum. Verified samples additionally pass shared checks for record completeness, image validity, answer-space consistency, multi-image alignment, and required metadata.

sections.title: 3.3 REAL-WORLD CURATION
sections.content: We construct the real-world evaluation set by curating samples from existing visual reasoning benchmarks and public datasets. Candidate samples are drawn from sources containing real images, videos, multi-view observations, and structured annotations (Fu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026; Ji et al., 2025; Yeh et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026; Pothiraj et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2026a). We select samples whose reasoning requirements align with those of the toy-game tasks, including fine-grained visual evidence, spatial structure, relational constraints, and state changes. For benchmark tasks that already meet the target reasoning requirements, we retain their original questions, answers, and evaluation protocols. Otherwise, we construct new evaluation samples from the source media and annotations while preserving the same reasoning requirements. For example, for IKEA Manuals at Work (Liu et al., 2024), we align assembly instructions with real assembly videos and construct multi-image questions from visually distinguishable states before and after an assembly step. All samples in the final set undergo automated consistency checks and manual review, and samples with ambiguous answers or insufficient visual evidence are removed.

sections.title: 3.4 BENCHMARK STATISTICS
sections.content: Game2Real-Dataset. Game2Real-Dataset contains 23,893 verified game samples across four capability groups, 18 toy-game tasks, and 65 QA families. It comprises 20,701 open-ended and 3,192 single-choice samples, with both single-image and multi-image inputs and 36,441 images in total. Game2Real-Bench. Game2Real-Bench contains 1,400 evaluation samples, including 1,000 toygame samples and 400 real-world samples. The toy-game set is generated independently from Game2Real-Dataset using disjoint random seeds and distinct layout configurations. We further use semantic fingerprints and image hashes to remove potential overlap. The set includes 600 openended and 400 single-choice questions. For the real-world set, we curate 400 samples to provide broad coverage across the four capability groups and their corresponding reasoning requirements. The Game2Real-Bench composition and representative examples are shown in Figure 2.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: Models. We evaluate 25 vision-language models, including 22 open-weight models and three proprietary frontier systems. The open-weight models span 2B to 35B total parameters and cover representative families including Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025), Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.8 (Qwen Team, 2026a), InternVL3.5 (Wang et al., 2025), Gemma4 (Team et al., 2026), GLM-4V (Hong et al., 2025), MiMo-VL (Yue et al., 2025), Ovis2.5 (Lu et al., 2025), NEO (Diao et al., 2026a), NEO-ov (Diao et al., 2026b), SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026c), and Step3-VL (Huang et al., 2026a). We additionally evaluate three proprietary frontier models GPT5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026), Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview (Google DeepMind, 2026), and Claude-Opus4.8 (Anthropic, 2026). Unless otherwise specified, all models use default inference configurations. Evaluation Protocol. All models are evaluated zero-shot using the same task instructions, source visual inputs, and questions. Open-weight models are evaluated through VLMEvalKit (Duan et al., 2024) using their official checkpoints and model-specific preprocessing, while proprietary models are accessed through their official APIs. No external tools or task-specific solvers are used during inference. For toy-game samples, model outputs are normalized according to each QA familys answer schema and scored by deterministic evaluators derived from the task rules. For real-world samples, we follow the original evaluation protocol when source benchmark provides standard evaluator and apply unified evaluation criteria to reconstructed samples. Current VLMs remain challenged on Game2Real-Bench. GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest overall score at 69.8%, while Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview and Claude-Opus-4.8 reach 59.6% and 53.7%, respectively. Toy-game tasks are more challenging and provide clearer separation between models. Most models achieve lower performance on the toy-game set than on the real-world set, with the difference being particularly visible among open-weight models. The toy-game evaluation also produces wider gaps between stronger and weaker systems. For example, the best proprietary and open-weight models differ by 16.3, 39.0, and 20.4 points on fine-grained perception, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning, respectively, while these gaps are much smaller on the corresponding real-world 6 Figure 3: Capability-wise game-to-real transfer with one-shot in-context learning. Compared with zero-shot evaluation, random game demonstrations improve constraint reasoning on average but reduce fine-grained perception accuracy for all four models on the 400 real-world targets. tasks. This difference may partly reflect the controlled nature of the toy-game tasks, where models must follow explicit rules and produce solutions that satisfy precisely defined states, constraints, and transitions. Real-world samples provide more familiar visual content and generally yield more compressed performance range. This contrast highlights the different roles of the two settings. Real-world tasks assess reasoning in natural visual contexts, while toy-game tasks provide finer discrimination among current VLMs under more explicitly specified reasoning requirements. Performance varies considerably across capabilities, with sequential planning showing the most consistent strength. Sequential planning yields the strongest performance for many models across both evaluation settings, and is the highest-scoring capability for 15 of the 25 models on the toy-game set and 17 on the real-world set. In contrast, the relative difficulty of the other capabilities changes across settings. Fine-grained perception produces the lowest average performance on the toy-game set, but becomes one of the stronger capabilities on real-world tasks. Constraint reasoning shows the opposite pattern more clearly among stronger models, remaining difficult and preserving visible gap between proprietary and open-weight systems. These results suggest that capability performance is not determined by the reasoning category alone, but also by how the underlying reasoning requirements are instantiated in each visual setting.

sections.title: 4.3 FINE-GRAINED ANALYSIS
sections.content: To better understand the relation between game tasks and real-world visual reasoning, we analyze model-level consistency across the two evaluation settings, game-to-real transfer through one-shot in-context learning, the effect of thinking mode, and representative failure cases. Game-to-real transfer with one-shot in-context learning. We study whether solved game examples can transfer to real-world visual reasoning through one-shot in-context learning. We evaluate four representative models on the same 400 real-world targets used in the zero-shot setting. We construct pool of 168 verified samples from Game2Real-Dataset covering 14 game tasks, and randomly assign one game demonstration to each target while balancing the four capabilities across the full set. We repeat the assignment with three random seeds and use the same demonstration-target pairs for all models. Each demonstration contains the game image and question followed only by its ground-truth final answer. All other evaluation settings remain unchanged. The effect of game demonstrations varies clearly across both capabilities and models, as shown in Figure 3. Constraint reasoning improves by 4.89 points on average, with Qwen3.5-9B increasing from 24.32% to 39.94%. These tasks require models to abstract visual observations into rules, relations, and valid configurations, so solved game example may help establish structured problemsolving context even when the demonstration comes from different task. Fine-grained perception shows the opposite pattern, decreasing by 4.92 points on average and declining for all four models. These tasks already achieve relatively high zero-shot performance and depend mainly on targetspecific visual evidence, for which an unrelated demonstration provides little additional information 7 Figure 4: Game-to-real performance correlation. Model performance across the game and real-world evaluations is strongly correlated. Figure 5: Thinking gains across model scales. Thinking improves overall score across all four models, with larger models benefiting more. and may introduce irrelevant context. The model-level results are also non-uniform. Qwen3.5-9B is the only model with an overall gain of 1.49 points, while Qwen3.8-27B changes by only 0.33 points, suggesting limited sensitivity to single random demonstration. The 2B and 4B models decrease overall, which may reflect greater difficulty in separating useful contextual cues from unrelated task information. Overall accuracy decreases by 1.34 points on average, indicating that game-to-real transfer is selective and depends on both the reasoning requirement and the model. Consistency between game and real-world evaluation. We examine whether the controlled game evaluation preserves the model-level performance differences observed on real-world visual reasoning tasks. This analysis covers all 25 models, with each model treated as one observation. For each model, we pair its overall score on the 1,000 game samples with its independently computed overall score on the 400 real-world samples. We then compute Pearson and Spearman correlations across the 25 model pairs. Pearson correlation measures the linear association between model scores in the two settings, while Spearman correlation measures whether their relative rankings are preserved. We obtain Pearson correlation of = 0.935 and Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.935, as shown in Figure 4. Both metrics indicate that the two evaluations preserve similar model-level performance patterns. Models with higher scores on the game evaluation generally also achieve higher scores on the real-world evaluation, and their relative ordering remains largely consistent across the two settings. This agreement suggests that, despite differences in visual content and task formulation, the game evaluation captures performance variation that is also reflected in real-world visual reasoning. Thinking improves performance across model families. We compare thinking and non-thinking configurations for four models from different families, covering both open-weight and proprietary systems. As shown in Figure 5, all four models improve on the full 1,400-sample benchmark. Qwen3.5-2B, Step3-VL-10B, and Gemma4-31B-it gain 6.2, 6.0, and 11.1 percentage points, respectively, while GPT-5.6-Sol gains 41.5 points, increasing from 28.3% to 69.8%. The larger gains of Gemma4-31B-it and GPT-5.6-Sol suggest that additional inference-time computation may be more useful for models with stronger visual reasoning capabilities. Such models may better use the extra reasoning budget to explore alternatives, verify intermediate states, and revise earlier decisions. The smaller gains of the other two models may partly reflect errors in visual understanding or the initial problem representation that additional reasoning steps alone cannot always correct. Failure Case Analysis. We examine failure cases across all tasks and summarize three recurring error patterns, illustrated by representative examples from Block Counting, Hexakai, and Mancala in Figure 6. Misinterpreting Spatial Structure. Models may form an incorrect spatial representation before reasoning begins. In Block Counting, they fail to recover hidden cubes and column structures from the 2D projection, leading to an incorrect 3D configuration before counting. Inconsistent Relational Reasoning. Models may identify the relevant structure initially but fail to preserve its relations during deduction. In Hexakai, Gemini-3.1-Pro changes constraint-line memberships, while Qwen3.8-27B eliminates candidates without verifying the relations. Unreliable State Updating. Models may follow sequence correctly for several steps but fail to apply required state transiFigure 6: Failure cases on Game2Real-Bench. Model reasoning traces are compared with verified solutions for Block Counting, Hexakai, and Mancala. These cases illustrate three recurring failures: misinterpreting spatial structure, inconsistent relational reasoning, and unreliable state updating. tion. In Mancala, Qwen3.8-27B tracks the board state through most of the trajectory but misses the capture update when its condition is satisfied. These cases illustrate how errors can arise at different stages of visual reasoning, from spatial representation to relation maintenance and state transition.

sections.title: 5 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Game2Real-Bench focuses on four capability groups and connects toy-game tasks with corresponding real-world visual reasoning settings. Several directions remain for future work. Broader task coverage. The current benchmark includes 18 toy-game tasks and 400 real-world samples. Although these tasks cover diverse reasoning requirements, they do not span the full range of visual reasoning in natural environments. Future extensions can include additional task types and richer visual settings while preserving the gamereal alignment principle. Broader transfer settings. Our transfer study focuses on one-shot in-context learning. Game2Real-Dataset provides nearly 24K verified game samples, which can support future studies of multi-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning for game-to-real transfer. Behavioral correspondence. The correlation between game and real-world performance reflects consistency at the model level, but does not establish that the two settings rely on the same internal reasoning processes. Further analysis can investigate how shared reasoning requirements are represented and used across the two settings.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce Game2Real-Bench, benchmark that pairs controlled toy-game tasks with real-world visual reasoning tasks to examine whether abilities revealed in toy games are reflected in real-world performance and can transfer across settings. Across 25 VLMs, toy-game and real-world performance is strongly correlated, while toy-game tasks are generally more challenging and provide clearer separation among current models. Capability-level results further show that shared reasoning requirements can exhibit different difficulty profiles when instantiated in the two settings. One-shot game-to-real in-context learning also reveals selective transfer, with constraint reasoning benefiting for several models while fine-grained perception consistently declines. We also study the effects of thinking mode and analyze representative failure cases. These results show that toy games provide an informative setting for probing real-world visual reasoning and cross-setting transfer. Together, Game2Real-Bench and Game2Real-Dataset provide verifiable evaluation framework and scalable data resource for advancing the study of game-to-real transfer in visual reasoning.

A.1 TASK TAXONOMY AND QA FORMULATION The 18 toy-game tasks are organized into four capability groups: Fine-grained Perception (C1), Spatial Reasoning (C2), Constraint Reasoning (C3), and Sequential Planning (C4). Each task is assigned to the group that best reflects its primary reasoning demand. Solving task may also involve other capabilities, such as perception during planning or constraint satisfaction in spatial reasoning. task defines game environment with explicit rules and solution criteria, while QA family specifies the reasoning target and output format within that task. For example, Rolling Cube includes questions about the top face, selected faces, or all six faces after the roll sequence, as well as face states at intermediate checkpoints. Each sample instantiates QA family with one or more visual observations, question, and verified answer. Its instructions specify the relevant notation, coordinate system, and output conventions. Table 2 summarizes the task coverage and sample counts for Game2Real-Dataset and the toy-game evaluation set of Game2Real-Bench. sections.content: We detail the construction pipeline through Rolling Cube, focusing on how the generator and verifier track physical faces and their sticker patterns. We then use an IKEA assembly example to show how aligned instructions and video frames become multi-image question with reference answer. B.1 PROCEDURAL GENERATION Initial face patterns. The generator samples 3 3 sticker grid for each of the six faces. Each grid contains all six symbols in the selected vocabulary, with three symbols appearing twice. During sampling, grids are compared under rotations and reflections to avoid equivalent patterns on separate faces. The evaluation uses geometric symbols; dataset construction also supports digits and letters. We retain the initial layouts and their vocabulary separately from the answers derived after rolling. Movement sequence and visual inputs. The generator samples start cell and extends path through orthogonally adjacent cells. Configuration profiles control the board size, number of rolls, and changes between horizontal and vertical movement. Proposed paths must remain within the board and satisfy the profiles turn and revisit conditions. Each movement represents 90 roll, not translation or an in-place rotation. The instance is rendered into two inputs: numbered path on the board and panel containing the six initial face layouts. Their roles and order are stated in the prompt, with the path and face grids preserved in the verification metadata. Queries and distractors. QA construction selects the requested checkpoint and world-facing side. Full-grid questions in Game2Real-Dataset require the entire oriented pattern; other variants query selected faces, the complete six-face state, or intermediate checkpoints. For six-option grid question, the distractor pool includes rotations and reflections of the target grid, alternative face states, and local symbol changes. Duplicate grids are removed before options are selected and shuffled. These alternatives distinguish an incorrect face from correct face with the wrong orientation. The validation interface removes declared answer labels and correctness flags before invoking the task checker. Rolling Cube reconstructs its result from initial faces and moves, rather than reading saved final layout or candidate-validity flag. Each option is parsed into 33 grid and compared with the recomputed Top grid. Acceptance requires exactly one valid option and agreement with the exported answer. The checker reuses the generators rotation and layout functions, verifying label-independent state recomputation under the shared simulation implementation. Auditing the exported question. Release checks address the interface between the state and the question: the two input images must have the correct roles, path markers must be distinguished from direction names, and face names must denote world-facing positions at the requested checkpoint. The stored layout, candidate order, and exported label must agree. For open-ended variants, the reference is also passed through the answer parser and evaluator to check field names and symbol normalization. The parser round trip checks output formatting, while state replay checks consistency with the implemented task dynamics. Other tasks and collection-level checks. Other tasks use the same separation between generation, answer checking, and export auditing. Object annotations support counting, constraint solvers check complete assignments, and dynamic tasks replay actions with their state-dependent effects. Uniqueness or optimality is checked when the task requires it; Rolling Cube instead specifies fixed sequence with determined outcome. Collection-level checks remove benchmarkdataset overlaps using semantic fingerprints and image hashes. B.3 REAL-WORLD CURATION AND GAME-TO-REAL ALIGNMENT Scope of gamereal alignment. Game2Real-Bench connects procedural games with real-world questions through shared reasoning requirements. Alignment guides curation and capability-level reporting rather than requiring one-to-one correspondence between tasks or samples. The two settings retain different visual evidence, rules, and answer spaces. For example, Cube Net and the IKEA assembly questions both relate two-dimensional specification to three-dimensional configuration. Their connection concerns spatial interpretation, while cube folding and assemblystate recognition retain distinct operations, input formats, and solution criteria. Primary annotations and task coverage. Each real-world sample has primary toy-task annotation recording its designated gamereal connection. This annotation is not an exhaustive list of the operations needed to solve the question. Likewise, capability labels identify primary demands rather than mutually exclusive skills: Rolling Cube is grouped under spatial reasoning but also requires sequential state tracking. The primary annotations cover 14 game task types, whereas the full toy-game evaluation retains all 18 tasks. The other four tasks have no retained real-world sample with that primary annotation. Accordingly, the full-suite correlation assesses model-level performance correspondence; it is not an estimate of the predictive value of each individual task link. Source-specific construction. Table 5 lists the real-world sources. We retain 246 original QA samples and lightly reformulate 72 while preserving their answers. New annotation-derived questions comprise 27 SPair-71k keypoint-matching samples and five IKEA assembly-state samples. 19 Another 50 SpatiaLQA samples retain the official tasks with restored action-content and precondition graphs. sections.title: C EVALUATION PROTOCOL
sections.content: We detail the inference configurations, model inputs, and scoring procedures for both evaluation settings. Shared prompt construction preserves task-specific output conventions, while reference answers and evaluator metadata remain separate from the target input supplied to each model. C.1 MODEL AND INFERENCE CONFIGURATIONS Model interfaces. Open-weight models are evaluated through VLMEvalKit adapters, with checkpoint, chat-template, and visual preprocessing settings determined by the corresponding run configuration (Duan et al., 2024). Proprietary models are accessed through API interfaces. Each model receives the source images and shared task prompt, without external tools, reference solutions, or task-specific solvers. Model-specific inference controls are summarized in Appendix D.4. Thinking-mode generation for Qwen. For Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.8 with thinking enabled, we use two-stage generation budget of 32k + 512 tokens. The initial stage allows up to 32k generated tokens. If this budget is exhausted without final answer, we continue the same attempt with an answer-format instruction and up to 512 additional tokens, without reference answers or evaluator feedback. Responses completed within the initial budget are evaluated directly. Both paths use the same answer normalization and scoring procedures. Controlled in-context evaluation. The one-shot analysis evaluates Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Qwen3.8-27B on the same 400 real-world targets. The controlled Qwen runner uses vLLM with native multi-turn conversations and model-specific custom prompts disabled  (Table 7)  . Paired zero-shot and one-shot evaluations retain the same configuration for each model, including the two-stage generation budget when thinking is enabled. The paired runs differ only in demonstration context, not in inference mode. Table 7: Configuration of the controlled Qwen in-context learning runner. Paired zero-shot and one-shot runs share these inference settings. In thinking mode, the additional answer budget is used only when the initial budget is exhausted without final answer. Setting Value Backend Sampling Top-p / top-k Thinking budget Custom prompts Disabled vLLM Disabled 0.95 / 20 32k tokens Setting Value Temperature Context limit Presence penalty Answer budget Answer stage 0 65,536 1.5 512 tokens Conditional C.2 PROMPTING AND INPUT FORMATTING Shared input construction. The ImageMixedQA and RealWorldFinal interfaces share one prompt builder. Each input contains the stored image sequence followed by text block with optional task instructions from the hint field, the question, available options, image-role instructions, and the answer-format suffix. The targets reference answers, accepted alternatives, and evaluator payloads are reserved for scoring and excluded from the prompt and its image-role descriptions. Image roles and answer candidates. The prompt distinguishes question and reference images from images that represent answer options. For example, Rolling Cube provides the board and roll sequence separately from the initial cube layout, whereas Cylinder Coloring supplies reference projections followed by candidate views. When candidates are supplied as separate images, the prompt explicitly maps their positions to option letters, preventing an image index from being confused with an answer label. When the options are textual, all supplied views remain question or reference images and are interpreted jointly in the stored order, with their task-specific roles preserved. Answer-format instructions. The shared suffix requests direct answer and ends with questiontype-specific instruction, as shown in the prompt box. Open-ended questions retain their requested schema, including field assignments, action sequences, rankings, and JSON objects. For example, 22 Shared answer instruction Answer directly. Do not explain your reasoning. For single-choice questions, answer with one option letter only, such as A. For multiple-answer questions, answer with all correct option letters separated by commas, such as A,C,E. For open questions, follow the required answer format exactly. Single-choice suffix: This is single-choice question. Return one option letter only. Open-ended suffix: This is an open question. Return only the requested structured answer. IKEA frame selections remain JSON arrays of frame labels rather than single-choice option letters. Output format and model-side thinking mode are configured separately at inference. One-shot conversation format. game demonstration is represented as user turn containing its images and question, followed by an assistant turn containing only its verified final answer. The real-world target is then supplied as new user turn using the same input construction as in zero-shot evaluation. Demonstrations therefore provide solved examples without additional reasoning traces or target annotations. The three assignments use seeds 11, 23, and 37, with identical demonstration target pairs across models. Only the demonstration context changes; the target images, question, answer schema, and scoring procedure remain the same across the paired evaluations. C.3 TOY-GAME ANSWER NORMALIZATION AND SCORING Schema-specific normalization. Toy-game predictions are evaluated against the answer schema attached to each sample. For the 400 single-choice questions, the answer is mapped to one of six valid option letters and compared with the reference label. For the 600 open-ended questions, deterministic parsers recover the requested values or actions and pass them to the corresponding task evaluator. Normalization is restricted to representations supported by that schema, such as whitespace, letter case, recognized symbol aliases, and equivalent field separators; it does not infer omitted values, repair an incorrect solution, or alter the submitted sequence of actions. Structured answers. For field-based outputs, the parser checks the complete set of requested keys and their associated values. Reordering independent field assignments is permitted, while missing fields, duplicate keys, and unexpected fields are rejected. Coordinate collections are normalized where their order is irrelevant, whereas checkpoint order, vector entries, and action sequences retain their prescribed meaning. For example, reversing the order of two named count fields does not change an answer, but reversing two moves can change the resulting state. The open-answer parser must consume the complete submitted answer, so unsupported wrappers and surrounding explanations are not silently ignored during schema validation to obtain matching answer. Task-grounded correctness. Attribute, count, and queried-state answers require all requested components to match their verified targets. Tasks admitting alternative solutions are instead checked against their executable rules. For KeyPath Quest and Growing Trail, the evaluator replays the submitted route, verifies legal transitions and goal completion, and checks its length against the stored optimum. Rush Exit similarly checks vehicle movements and the minimum number of commands, rather than the total distance traveled. Laser verifies the submitted mirror configuration through ray simulation, including the relay order, target entry, and optimality conditions specified by the task. Order-sensitive state updates. Pipe predictions are evaluated as ordered rotation sequences. The evaluator applies each operation to the current state, propagates water, and updates which pipes are locked before considering the next operation. It therefore does not reorder submitted plan to make an otherwise invalid sequence succeed. Mancala evaluation checks the requested board state and event fields against the replayed transitions, including sowing, captures, extra turns, and terminal sweeping. These checks require both the requested board components and the event flags to agree with the replayed state; partially correct configuration does not receive credit. Sample scores. Each toy-game sample receives binary score. prediction is correct only when it satisfies the answer schema and all required task conditions, including optimality when requested. valid alternative solution can therefore receive full credit without matching the stored canonical answer verbatim. Invalid or incomplete answers receive zero, and intermediate agreement is not awarded partial credit. Parser and simulator diagnostics are retained separately for error analysis. C.4 REAL-WORLD EVALUATION PROTOCOLS Reference-independent answer extraction. Real-world responses are first converted to the output type specified by each sample. The extractor removes recognized reasoning blocks and output wrappers, prioritizes explicit final-answer markers, and recovers structured values from JSON or Python-style lists when applicable. For choice and numeric questions, type-specific fallbacks recover candidate letter or number when no explicit final-answer field is available. This stage uses the response and question-side information, without access to reference answers or accepted alternatives. The extracted prediction is then passed to the appropriate evaluator in Table 8. Table 8: Scoring rules for the 400 real-world samples. Counts refer to the final selected set. All subsets use binary correctness except SpatiaLQA, which contributes normalized graph score. Subset or answer type Samples Scoring criterion Single-choice subsets GQA short answers CAPTURe-real counts VisualTrans and IKEA frame selection SSI-Bench rankings ReasonMap routes SpatiaLQA dependency graphs 236 Exact option-label match. 12 Normalized short-answer match. 30 Exact count correctness. 8 Exact selected labels, ignoring order. 50 Exact match of the full ranking. 14 Match to an accepted structured route. 50 Mean of content and precondition F1. Total 400 Choice, short-answer, and counting tasks. Single-choice predictions are compared with the reference option label. Short answers are compared after text normalization, and counting questions require the predicted count to match the reference. When sample contains multiple accepted answers, matching any one of them is sufficient. For the CAPTURe-real subset, this is an adaptation to exact count correctness rather than the original sMAPE metric (Pothiraj et al., 2025). The count remains discrete target, with no tolerance-based partial credit for approximate answers. Frame selection and structural ranking. The reconstructed IKEA questions require selecting frames that match the post-step state indicated by an assembly instruction. Their frame labels are compared without regard to order, as are the corresponding multi-frame selections from VisualTrans. The complete selection must match the reference; missing or additional labels are incorrect. In contrast, SSI-Bench requires an ordered permutation of structural elements. We use its taskwise exact-match criterion, rather than pairwise ordering accuracy (Yang et al., 2026). Output normalization preserves the ranking, including any tie-breaking convention stated in the original question. Transit-route answers. ReasonMap responses are parsed into ordered route sections containing the line name, departure and arrival stops, and any requested intermediate-stop counts or lists. The evaluator normalizes textual representations and compares the complete route with the accepted reference routes. Section order and the requested stop information are retained during comparison. This produces binary structured-route score for Game2Real-Bench, rather than reproducing ReasonMaps full correctness and route-quality evaluation or its graded map score (Feng et al., 2026). SpatiaLQA step content and dependencies. We adopt SpatiaLQAs distinction between stepcontent correctness and precondition correctness (Xie et al., 2026a). Each answer represents an execution plan as graph whose nodes contain action descriptions and whose edges encode prerequisite steps. Predicted and reference steps are aligned through binary correspondence matrix and maximum-cardinality one-to-one matching. Content precision and recall count matched, extra, and missing steps. After aligning step identities, precondition precision and recall compare the predicted and reference dependency edges. Changing step identifiers or JSON key order does not change the plan, provided that its action contents and dependencies are preserved. The benchmark implementation uses rule-based action, object, and contextual matching at threshold of 0.72, replacing the official GPT-4o-based correspondence stage. Content and precondition F1 scores are then computed from the resulting step alignment. For sample i, the benchmark uses si = (Fc,i + Fp,i)/2, where Fc,i and Fp,i denote content and precondition F1, respectively. This 24 averaging defines our benchmark-level aggregation, rather than an additional official SpatiaLQA metric. Predictions with no matched steps receive zero and remain in the evaluation denominator. Aggregation across tasks and settings. For any evaluation set S, we report Score(S) = 100 S1 (cid:80) iS si. Each real-world capability contains 100 samples, so its overall score is also the unweighted mean of the four capability scores. The joint benchmark score instead averages over all 1,400 samples, assigning weights of 1,000/1,400 and 400/1,400 to the toy-game and real-world sets. All selected samples remain in the denominator. This quantity is accuracy for binary-scored subsets and an average normalized score when the SpatiaLQA graph scores are included.
